name: Expansion-history models fitted to the Pantheon+ supernova Hubble diagram
description: Propose a parametric expansion history E(z) = H(z)/H0 with at most six parameters and fit it to the 1,580 Pantheon+ Type Ia supernova light curves with zHD > 0.01 (the 1,590-object cosmology sample minus the ten Cepheid-host calibrators) (corrected apparent magnitudes and the full statistical plus systematic covariance). The absolute magnitude is profiled analytically; the score is the minimum chi-squared, lower is better. Flat LambdaCDM with a fitted matter density is reported for comparison.

sources.locator: Brout et al. 2022, The Pantheon+ Analysis: Cosmological Constraints; Section 2 (data), Section 3 (likelihood with the STAT+SYS covariance, zHD > 0.01 cut).
Pantheon+SH0ES.dat and Pantheon+SH0ES_STAT+SYS.cov, fetched by scripts/prepare_science_data.py and pinned by SHA-256.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; mathematical constructions or locally generated synthetic instances.

execution.interface: expansion(z, theta) -> array E(z) = H(z)/H0 for an array of redshifts z >= 0 (positive, finite; E(0) should be 1); initial_theta() -> initial parameter vector (1 to 6 values); bounds() -> list of (low, high) per parameter. The evaluator fits theta to the Pantheon+ Hubble diagram (zHD > 0.01 and no Cepheid calibrators: 1,580 light curves, STAT+SYS covariance) with the absolute magnitude profiled analytically and H0 = 70 fixed for the distance scale; score is the minimum chi-squared (lower is better). Flat LambdaCDM (fitted Omega_m) chi-squared is reported for comparison.

limitations: Real measurements: the data are the public Pantheon+ release, fetched at prepare time (network), not redistributed.
The likelihood profiles the absolute magnitude and fixes H0 = 70 for the distance scale, so only the shape of E(z) is constrained; the SH0ES Cepheid calibrators are excluded.

A lower chi-squared than LambdaCDM with more parameters is not by itself evidence for new physics; model comparison needs an information criterion or Bayesian evidence, which the evaluator reports the ingredients for (chi-squared and parameter count).

name: PFHub spinodal decomposition integration
description: evolve_composition(initial_field, parameters, times) -> array (len(times),N,N). Integrate dc/dt=M*L[f'(c)-kappa*L(c)] using the specified second-order periodic discrete Laplacian on [0,200)^2; f=rho*(c-alpha)^2*(c-beta)^2 with alpha=.3,beta=.7,rho=5,M=5,kappa=2. Score candidate wall time only when RMSE<=2e-5 versus independent DOP853, mass drift<1e-9 and discrete free energy never increases. Two fixed meshes 48 and 64, published initial condition and a phase-shift adaptation, times 1,5,20. These are explicit short-horizon, fixed-mesh adaptations, not a reproduction of PFHub equilibrium results.

The best known construction is Exoo's 42-vertex graph (R(5,5) >= 43) and Angeltveit and McKay proved R(5,5) <= 46, so the exact value is open. The seed is the Paley graph on 37 vertices, verified (5,5)-free by the evaluator.

sources.locator: Angeltveit and McKay, R(5,5) <= 46: the current upper bound and a summary of the lower bound 43 (Exoo 1989).
Radziszowski, Small Ramsey Numbers (dynamic survey): R(5,5) bounds 43..46.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; mathematical constructions or locally generated synthetic instances.

evaluation.benchmark: Ramsey graphs for R(5,5): large graphs with no K5 and no independent 5-set
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct() -> (n, edges): the number of vertices and a list of (i, j) pairs with 0 <= i < j < n. The graph must contain no clique of size CLIQUE and no independent set of size INDEPENDENT; n must be at most MAX_VERTICES. Score: n, maximized (each valid graph proves R(CLIQUE, INDEPENDENT) > n).

limitations: Exoo's 42-vertex graph is not embedded; the evaluator only certifies candidate graphs, so the reference label is none.
A valid graph on 43 or more vertices would refute the conjecture R(5,5) = 43 and must be independently verified.

name: Snake-in-the-box in the 10-cube
description: Construct a snake that is as long as possible in the hypercube Q_10: the graph whose vertices are the integers 0 to 2^10 - 1, two of them adjacent when they differ in exactly one bit. A snake is an induced path: consecutive vertices of the path are adjacent, and no two vertices that are not consecutive on it are adjacent.

sources.locator: T. Ace, Snake-in-the-Box lower bounds: the longest snake listed for dimension 10, with a sample snake
A Census of New Snake-in-the-Box Records (the records of July 2026, source of the first version of this task)
Table 1 (lower bounds for dimensions 9 to 13: 191, 379, 746, 1476, 2924) and Definition 1: snake = induced path, length = number of edges.

execution.interface: construct() -> list of at least two distinct integers in [0, 2**10): the vertices of the path in order. Consecutive vertices must differ in exactly one bit, and any two non-consecutive ones in at least two bits. Score: number of edges of the path (the number of vertices minus one), maximized.
notes: No data files.

limitations: The records come from searches tuned for this problem (cube-surgery annealing, beam search with local rerouting).

The records move: in 2026 the leaderboard recorded improvements in every dimension of this family, several within weeks of each other. The record is the state on the day of the record validation and will fall behind.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.reason: Both papers have the longest induced path in the hypercube as their main objective; the 2026 paper set the records of July 2026 for dimensions 10 to 13 (others have lengthened those of dimensions 11 to 13 since), and the 2016 paper held the earlier bounds for dimensions 11 to 13; the verifier checks the induced-path property exactly.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Construct the longest induced path (snake) in the 10-dimensional hypercube Q_10, measured in edges.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The snake-in-the-box problem comes from coding theory (Kautz 1958, error-detecting unit-distance Gray codes) and is a standard test of combinatorial search; the maximum length is proven only up to dimension 8, so every longer snake in dimension 9 and above is a new lower bound.

source_specification.description: Construct a snake that is as long as possible in the hypercube Q_13: the graph whose vertices are the integers 0 to 2^13 - 1, two of them adjacent when they differ in exactly one bit. A snake is an induced path: consecutive vertices of the path are adjacent, and no two vertices that are not consecutive on it are adjacent.
source_specification.source_locator: T. Ace, Snake-in-the-Box lower bounds: the longest snake listed for dimension 13, with a sample snake
source_specification.execution_notes: No data files.

name: Sorting network on 19 inputs
description: Construct a sorting network on 19 wires with as few comparators as possible. A comparator (i, j) with i < j compares the values on wires i and j and puts the smaller one on wire i and the larger one on wire j; the comparators are applied in the given order. The network must sort every input, that is, leave the values in non-decreasing order along wires 0 to 18.

sources.locator: Using Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks
Codish et al. (2015), Sorting Networks: to the End and Back Again: new networks for 17 to 20 inputs, mainly about depth (layers), so not evidence for the size objective.
Ehlers and Mueller (2014), Faster Sorting Networks for 17, 19 and 20 Inputs: depth upper bounds, not size.
Depth-13 Sorting Networks for 28 Channels (2025): depth upper bounds for 27 and 28 inputs, not size.

execution.interface: construct() -> list of comparators (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < 19, in the order in which they are applied (at least one). The network is verified on all 2^19 inputs of zeros and ones, which is equivalent to sorting every input. Score: number of comparators, minimized (the depth is not scored).
notes: No data files.

limitations: Exact 0-1 verification over all 2^19 inputs, in blocks of 2^24.
SorterHunter and symmetry-based searches have worked on these sizes for years.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

name: Spherical code, 100 points in dimension 3
description: Place 100 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 100 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 100 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/100, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (100, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/100, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.reason: Both papers have the densest packing of n equal circles on a sphere, for whole ranges of n, as their main objective; the task poses the same problem for one n.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 100 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 100 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. Optimal arrangements are proven only up to 14 points and for 24 (a proof for 15 is claimed in a 2026 preprint), so for the sizes of this family the best known packings come from computer search and a larger minimum angle is a new best packing.

name: Spherical code, 18 points in dimension 3
description: Place 18 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 18 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 18 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 18 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 18 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. name: Spherical code, 46 points in dimension 3
description: Place 46 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 46 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 46 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/46, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (46, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/46, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 46 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 46 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. name: Spherical code, 55 points in dimension 3
description: Place 55 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 55 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 55 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/55, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (55, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/55, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 55 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 55 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. Optimal arrangements are proven only up to 14 points and for 24 (a proof for 15 is claimed in a 2026 preprint), so for the sizes of this family the best known packings come from computer search and a larger minimum angle is a new best packing.

name: Spherical code, 64 points in dimension 3
description: Place 64 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 64 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 64 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/64, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (64, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/64, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 64 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 64 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. name: Spherical code, 82 points in dimension 3
description: Place 82 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 82 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 82 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 82 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 82 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

The paper's searches reach 72 points in R^4 and 50 points in R^5 and report three improved codes in R^4 (40, 68 and 71 points); the task family goes to 130 points, so its larger sizes pose the paper's problem beyond the sizes the paper searched.
papers.primary_goal: Find good spherical codes of N points in R^n by energy minimisation from many random starts (dimensions 3 to 8), prove that the codes found exist exactly by writing their inner products as algebraic numbers, and catalogue them.

source_specification.execution_notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/4/65, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

name: Spherical code, 66 points in dimension 4
description: Place 66 points on the unit sphere in R^4 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (a spherical code). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 4, 66 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 4, 66 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
Finding and Investigating Exact Spherical Codes
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/4/66, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (66, 4): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/4/66, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.reason: The paper's main objective is to find the best spherical codes of N points in R^n by computer search, in dimensions 4 and 5 among others, and to show that the codes it finds exist exactly; the task poses the same problem for one N.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 66 points on the unit sphere of R^4 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 108 points on the unit sphere of R^5 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. The paper's searches reach 72 points in R^4 and 50 points in R^5 and report three improved codes in R^4 (40, 68 and 71 points); the task family goes to 130 points, so its larger sizes pose the paper's problem beyond the sizes the paper searched.
papers.primary_goal: Find good spherical codes of N points in R^n by energy minimisation from many random starts (dimensions 3 to 8), prove that the codes found exist exactly by writing their inner products as algebraic numbers, and catalogue them.

source_specification.name: Spherical code, 120 points in dimension 5
source_specification.description: Place 120 points on the unit sphere in R^5 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (a spherical code). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.
source_specification.dataset: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/120, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).
source_specification.source_locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 5, 120 points
source_specification.execution_notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/120, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

name: Spherical code, 121 points in dimension 5
description: Place 121 points on the unit sphere in R^5 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (a spherical code). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 5, 121 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 5, 121 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
Finding and Investigating Exact Spherical Codes
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/121, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (121, 5): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/121, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. science_relevance.reason: The paper's main objective is to find the best spherical codes of N points in R^n by computer search, in dimensions 4 and 5 among others, and to show that the codes it finds exist exactly; the task poses the same problem for one N.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 121 points on the unit sphere of R^5 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 45 points on the unit sphere of R^5 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

The paper's searches reach 72 points in R^4 and 50 points in R^5 and report three improved codes in R^4 (40, 68 and 71 points); the task family goes to 130 points, so its larger sizes pose the paper's problem beyond the sizes the paper searched.
papers.primary_goal: Find good spherical codes of N points in R^n by energy minimisation from many random starts (dimensions 3 to 8), prove that the codes found exist exactly by writing their inner products as algebraic numbers, and catalogue them.

source_specification.execution_notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/58, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

name: Spherical code, 59 points in dimension 5
description: Place 59 points on the unit sphere in R^5 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (a spherical code). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 5, 59 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 5, 59 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
Finding and Investigating Exact Spherical Codes
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

requirements.datasets: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/59, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (59, 5): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/5/59, which only the record validation reads (scripts/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.reason: The paper's main objective is to find the best spherical codes of N points in R^n by computer search, in dimensions 4 and 5 among others, and to show that the codes it finds exist exactly; the task poses the same problem for one N.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 59 points on the unit sphere of R^5 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

Finding and Investigating Exact Spherical Codes
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

science_relevance.reason: The paper's main objective is to find the best spherical codes of N points in R^n by computer search, in dimensions 4 and 5 among others, and to show that the codes it finds exist exactly; the task poses the same problem for one N.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 82 points on the unit sphere of R^5 whose smallest pairwise angle is as large as possible, that is a spherical code of maximal minimum angle; the reference is the best code known for this size, as listed in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Maximising the minimum angle of n points on a sphere is the Tammes problem (dimension 3, from the packing of pollen-grain apertures) and, in higher dimension, the spherical code problem of coding theory and sphere packing. Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

Optimality is proven only for few n (n <= 14 and 24 in R^3, with a proof for 15 claimed in 2026, and a handful of special codes in R^4 and R^5), so the listed codes for larger n are the best known, not proven, and a larger minimum angle would be a new best code.

name: TDC ADMET AMES
description: Predict whether a compound is mutagenic in the Ames test (1) or not (0) from its molecular structure, given as a SMILES string (endpoint AMES of the Therapeutics Data Commons ADMET benchmark group). The measured compounds are split by molecular scaffold into a training, a validation and a test part. The test part is fixed; the candidate is run five times (seeds 1 to 5), each time with a different division of the other compounds into training and validation. It receives the training and validation compounds with their values and the test compounds without, and returns one prediction per test compound. Each of the five runs is a separate process that receives only these arguments: it cannot read the evaluator's files, start other processes or open network connections, and it has 700 seconds. The score is the area under the ROC curve on the test compounds, averaged over the five runs; higher is better.

source_specification.name: TDC ADMET CYP3A4_Veith
source_specification.description: Predict whether a compound inhibits the drug-metabolising enzyme cytochrome P450 3A4 (1) or not (0) from its molecular structure, given as a SMILES string (endpoint CYP3A4_Veith of the Therapeutics Data Commons ADMET benchmark group). The measured compounds are split by molecular scaffold into a training, a validation and a test part. The test part is fixed; the candidate is run five times (seeds 1 to 5), each time with a different division of the other compounds into training and validation. It receives the training and validation compounds with their values and the test compounds without, and returns one prediction per test compound. Each of the five runs is a separate process that receives only these arguments: it cannot read the evaluator's files, start other processes or open network connections, and it has 700 seconds. The score is the area under the precision-recall curve on the test compounds, with class 1 as the positive class, averaged over the five runs; higher is better.

execution.interface: integrate(counts, batch_labels) -> finite cells x dimensions embedding, 1<=dimensions<=128. No cell-type labels supplied. Transductive evaluation. This is an adapted public scIB protocol, not reproduction of Station private scores.

provenance.note: New local evaluator and seed based on cited source specifications; official data are reused.

limitations: Measured scIB human-pancreas study:1000 hash-selected cells and500variable genes from raw-count layer,9genuine technology batches. Transductive local metrics, no fullscIB/Station score reproduction or cross-study claim.
Canonical Station upgrade using an explicitly adapted public scIB-style60/40 score. Does not reproduce the private Station evaluator or complete scIB metric suite; no trajectory conservation claim.
Public source subsets are development-visible. Freeze candidates before evaluating on additional independently chosen studies/instances; trusted candidate execution is not a security sandbox.
Improving this benchmark is a scientific-method result; it does not alone establish a new biological discovery.

name: Thomson problem, N = 10
description: Place 10 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.
J. J. Thomson (1904), On the structure of the atom: the corpuscle model that gave the problem its name (rings of corpuscles in a charged sphere; the surface problem is the later idealisation).
Schwartz (2013), The Five-Electron Case of Thomson's Problem: computer-assisted proof for N = 5; outside the N range of this family.
Erber and Hockney (1997), Complex Systems: Equilibrium Configurations of N Equal Charges on a Sphere (2 <= N <= 112), Adv. Chem. Phys.: extended tables.

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (10, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid, and so are two points that coincide). Score: sum over all pairs of points of 1/(Euclidean distance), minimized.
notes: No data files.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.
The record has 9 decimals; a result counts as an improvement only below it by more than 1e-8.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 10 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 103
description: Place 103 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 199 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 20
description: Place 20 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.
J. J. Thomson (1904), On the structure of the atom: the corpuscle model that gave the problem its name (rings of corpuscles in a charged sphere; the surface problem is the later idealisation).
Schwartz (2013), The Five-Electron Case of Thomson's Problem: computer-assisted proof for N = 5; outside the N range of this family.
Erber and Hockney (1997), Complex Systems: Equilibrium Configurations of N Equal Charges on a Sphere (2 <= N <= 112), Adv. Chem. Phys.: extended tables.

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (20, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid, and so are two points that coincide). Score: sum over all pairs of points of 1/(Euclidean distance), minimized.
notes: No data files.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.
The record has 9 decimals; a result counts as an improvement only below it by more than 1e-8.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 27 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 272
description: Place 272 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 306 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 31
description: Place 31 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.
J. J. Thomson (1904), On the structure of the atom: the corpuscle model that gave the problem its name (rings of corpuscles in a charged sphere; the surface problem is the later idealisation).

Erber and Hockney (1997), Complex Systems: Equilibrium Configurations of N Equal Charges on a Sphere (2 <= N <= 112), Adv. Chem. Phys.: extended tables.

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (31, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid, and so are two points that coincide). Score: sum over all pairs of points of 1/(Euclidean distance), minimized.
notes: No data files.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 33 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 334

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 36 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 37
description: Place 37 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere

Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Erber and Hockney (global search for N equal charges on a sphere) and Wales and Ulker (the global minima that the table of record energies reproduces) have the Thomson problem for many N as their main objective; the evaluator scores the Coulomb energy of N points on the unit sphere.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find the arrangement of 392 unit point charges on the unit sphere with the smallest Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs (the Thomson problem).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Thomson problem is the classical model of repelling charges confined to a sphere, which Thomson posed in his 1904 atom model and which now serves as a model for spherical crystals and shells; its energy landscape has exponentially many local minima, so global minima beyond N around 100 are putative. Only a few N (2 to 6 and 12) are rigorously proven, so a lower energy would be a new putative global minimum.

papers.title: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the minimum-energy configuration of N charges (the sum of 1/distance); this paper's search tables are an early record source for small N, while the task's N is larger in most cases.
papers.primary_goal: Find, by numerical minimisation, equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere and their energies.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
papers.task_relation: The Cambridge Cluster Database table of global minima that carries the paper's name is the source of the smallest known energies (Wikipedia reproduces it); the task asks to lower the energy for a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Characterise putative global minima of the Thomson problem and the structure and dynamics of the resulting spherical crystals.

papers.title: Defect motifs for spherical topologies
papers.task_relation: Its configurations are also reproduced in the Cambridge Cluster Database; the task asks to lower the energy of a given N.
papers.primary_goal: Study the defect motifs of low-energy configurations on the sphere, including the Thomson problem, extending the global-minimum search to larger N.

name: Thomson problem, N = 40

name: Thomson problem, N = 88
description: Place 88 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).

Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem

Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.
